# Lighting-Specific Compositing
## Overview
Lighting-Specific Compositing encompasses techniques that modify the standard front-to-back compositing equation to incorporate lighting effects, multi-channel illumination, geometric boundary enhancement, and shadow handling directly into the accumulation step [G]. It sets itself apart from [Pre-Integration Lookup](2854-pre-integration-lookup.md) (which approximates integration via texture lookups) and [Binary Swap Compositing](3264-binary-swap-compositing.md) (which focuses on parallel reduction structures), as it specifically addresses the illumination model within the compositing loop [G].

## Shared principles
This family modifies the standard compositing loop detailed in [Compositing and Blending](2515-compositing-and-blending.md) by computing lighting-specific contributions per sample or per channel before blending them into the accumulator [G]. Instead of using raw transfer function outputs, each method derives modified color $\Delta C_i$ and opacity $\Delta \alpha_i$ terms that encode illumination effects, shadowing, or geometric cues [G]. Early ray termination remains applicable when the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold [G].

## Subtopics

### [Incremental Blending for In-scattering](2880-incremental-blending-for-in-scattering.md)
Approximates volumetric light scattering by accumulating scattered light from discrete directions. It sets itself apart from standard compositing by replacing the sample's emitted color with a directionally averaged in-scattering term, and from [Intermixing](5139-intermixing.md) by explicitly managing the angular discretization of the scattering sphere through an iterative blending process rather than a single pass. Choose this when global illumination effects are needed without full path tracing costs.

### [Intermixing](5139-intermixing.md)
Renders multi-channel volume data by evaluating illumination per channel and combining results during accumulation. It sets itself apart from image-level intermixing by preserving correct depth-based occlusion between channels. Choose this for visualizing complex interactions between distinct data sources (e.g., tissue types).

### [Boundary Enhancement](8071-boundary-enhancement.md)
Improves boundary visibility by modulating opacity based on geometric cues (silhouettes). It sets itself apart from [Incremental Blending for In-scattering](2880-incremental-blending-for-in-scattering.md) (which handles light transport) and [Phong Shading with Volume Rendering](12805-phong-shading-with-volume-rendering.md) (which handles surface orientation lighting) by focusing instead on structural definition. Choose this to enhance edge definition in volumes.

### [Phong Shading with Volume Rendering](12805-phong-shading-with-volume-rendering.md)
Applies Phong lighting (diffuse/specular) to volume samples using gradient-based normals. It sets itself apart from the standard composite shader by incorporating gradient-based surface normals and lighting calculations into the color contribution before compositing, thereby adding surface-like shading cues to the volumetric data. Choose this for surface-like appearance in volumetric data.

### Shadow Catcher Compositing
A technique for rendering shadow catchers where the camera sees the background darkened by the ratio of visible to total direct light, with alpha carrying shadow opacity [S1, unofficial]. The implementation darkens the background by this ratio and stores shadow opacity in the alpha channel on a transparent background [S1, unofficial]. A key pitfall is that indirect rays must still see the ground to ensure correct global illumination interaction [S1, unofficial].

### Contour Rendering Compositing
A compositing step for contour rendering that uses Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) or Local Maximum Intensity Projection (LMIP) to combine ray samples [S2, unofficial]. The process performs classification and shading for all ray samples, then composites using MIP (max intensity) or LMIP to prevent stronger contours from hiding weaker, closer contours [S2, unofficial].

### Light Value Blending
Blends four light values (a, b, c, d) into a single packed light value, replacing any zero values with the fourth value before averaging [S3, unofficial]. The steps are: if a == 0, set a = d; if b == 0, set b = d; if c == 0, set c = d; return ((a + b + c + d) >> 2) & 0xFF00FF [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The separation of volume rendering into classification, shading, and compositing stages allows lighting-specific modifications to be applied during the compositing phase [S2, unofficial]. Shadow catcher compositing, which darkens the background based on visible direct light ratios, is supported in modern rendering engines alongside physical sky models and IES light controls [S1, unofficial].
